definition: Distributed Artificial Intelligence (DAI) (also called Decentralized Artificial Intelligence) is a melding of artificial intelligence with distributed computing.
details: From artificial intelligence comes the theory and technology for constructing or analyzing an intelligent system. But where artificial intelligence uses psychology as a source of ideas, inspiration, and metaphor, DAI uses sociology, economics, and management science for inspiration. Where the focus of artificial intelligence is on the individual, the focus of DAI is on the group. Distributed computing provides the computational substrate on which this group focus can occur. Using techniques from artificial intelligence, communication theory, control theory, and interaction theory, it produces a cooperative solution to problems by a decentralized group of computational entities (agents). DAI is closely related to and a predecessor of the field of multi-agent systems. They are distinguished generally by multi-agent systems being open, where the entities might arise from different interests and have individual goals, and distributed artificial-intelligence systems, where the entities have common goals. There are numerous applications and tools.

explainer.lead: Distributed artificial intelligence studies how a decentralized group of computational agents can solve a problem together rather than relying on one central intelligent system. It combines AI with distributed computing and draws inspiration about group behavior from sociology, economics, and management science.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a team searching for a lost dog: each person checks a different area, shares what they find, and works toward the same goal. Distributed artificial intelligence gives computer programs a similar job, letting separate agents cooperate instead of making one program do everything. The teamwork happens across connected computers.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer applying DAI designs agents that run on distributed computers, exchange information, and coordinate toward a shared goal. The computational substrate and the agents' communication and control matter alongside their individual problem-solving behavior. DAI is most closely aligned with cooperative systems whose entities share goals, unlike open multi-agent systems where participants may have different interests and individual goals.
tiers.paperLevel: DAI is cooperative problem solving by a decentralized set of computational entities, or agents, using AI with communication, control, and interaction theory on a distributed-computing substrate. Its analytical focus is the group rather than the individual, with social organization serving as a source of inspiration. It is closely related to and a predecessor of multi-agent systems; DAI is generally distinguished by common agent goals, whereas multi-agent systems may be open and contain agents with differing interests and individual goals.

explainer.example: Suppose three delivery robots must move packages through a building without one robot controlling the others. Each handles part of the workload and communicates with the others so their routes and handoffs support the shared goal of completing all deliveries.
explainer.intuition: One agent does not need to know or do everything. Separate agents can contribute parts of a solution and coordinate their actions so the group achieves a common objective.
howItWorks: Give the decentralized agents a common goal.
Run them on a distributed-computing substrate rather than as one centralized system.
Let the agents communicate and coordinate their actions.
Combine their contributions into a cooperative solution.
explainer.whyItMatters: It shifts AI from modeling an individual problem solver to designing cooperative behavior in a group. That perspective links intelligent systems with distributed computing and helped lead to the field of multi-agent systems.
misconceptions: DAI is not simply running one AI program on several computers.
It is not identical to every multi-agent system: DAI agents generally share goals.
Its focus is cooperation by the group, not making one agent more intelligent.
